pos: n. (Katharina von Bora, 1499–1552, wife of Martin Luther)
etymology: Greek Aikaterine, through Latin Katharina; von Bora, of the Saxon noble family of Bora.
biblical_def: Katharina von Bora was placed in a convent as a child, escaped it in a herring wagon with eleven other nuns in 1523, and two years later married Martin Luther. For the next twenty-one years she ran the Black Cloister at Wittenberg: a household of children, students, boarders, relatives, guests, a brewery, gardens, fishponds, livestock and a farm at Zulsdorf, with her husband's income unreliable and his hospitality unlimited. Luther called her his lord Katie and meant it as the compliment it is. The Reformation's recovery of marriage for ministers was not a theory that stayed on paper; it produced this house, and the parsonage that half of Protestant Europe would know for four centuries is modelled on it. Solomon describes the office without flattery and without condescension: every wise woman buildeth her house (Pro 14:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines housewifery as the business of the mistress of a family, and household as those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family.
webster_full: HOUSE'WIFERY, n. The business of the mistress of a family; female management of domestic concerns.
HOUSE'HOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; those who belong to a family.
CON'VENT, n. A body of monks or nuns; the house occupied by a community of religious recluses.
PAR'SONAGE, n. The house appropriated to the residence of a parson; the glebe and house belonging to a parish.
scriptures: Pro 14:1
Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands.
The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil.
Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.

Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work.
corruption_summary: A nun out of a convent in a herring wagon, and the first Protestant parsonage.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse comes from two directions at once. One party reduces Katharina to a housekeeper and treats the Reformation as a story about men; the other recruits her as an early feminist and resents the household as a cage. Neither reads what she actually did. She managed a large and complicated estate under constant financial strain, which is work requiring judgment, authority and nerve, and Scripture assigns it honour accordingly.

The principle to recover is that the household is a real sphere of dominion, entrusted and accountable, and that Scripture praises its competent management. “Every wise woman buildeth her house” (Pro 14:1). The husband's dependence is total and stated as such: “The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil” (Pro 31:11). And the catalogue of a godly woman's works in Paul is domestic from beginning to end: “if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers” (1Ti 5:10).

pos: n. (Idelette de Bure, c. 1500–1549, wife of John Calvin)
etymology: Germanic Idela, a diminutive of names in Id-, labour; French de Bure, of Bure, a Flemish place-name.
biblical_def: Idelette de Bure was a widow of Liege with two children when Calvin married her at Strasbourg in 1540. Her first husband had been an Anabaptist whom Calvin had helped to bring back from that error. For nine years she kept Calvin's house through his illnesses, the plague years, and the constant traffic of refugees through Geneva; their only son died within days of birth. She died in 1549, and Calvin wrote to Viret that he had lost the best companion of his life, who would have followed him into exile and into death. He never remarried. The dictionary records her because she is the whole evidence for something the caricature of Calvin cannot accommodate, and because Scripture counts a faithful wife among the Lord's plainest mercies (Pro 31:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines widow as a woman who has lost her husband by death, and helpmeet as a helper, a suitable companion.
webster_full: WID'OW, n. A woman who has lost her husband by death.
HELP'ER, n. One that helps, aids or assists; an assistant; an auxiliary.
COMPAN'ION, n. One who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates and converses.
BEREAVE'MENT, n. Deprivation, particularly by the loss of a friend by death.
scriptures: Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Rom 14:8
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.
corruption_summary: Nine years in Calvin's house, and he never remarried.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the popular portrait of Calvin as a cold administrator, which survives only by ignoring his letters. The man who wrote about Idelette's death was not cold, and the household she kept was full of sick guests and displaced Frenchmen. The record is short because she wrote nothing for publication, which is the ordinary case with the women of this period and not a measure of their weight.

The principle to recover is that the quiet spirit is not a lesser ornament but is valued by God at a stated price. “But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:4). The praise is given by those who lived with her: “Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her” (Pro 31:28).

pos: n. (Wibrandis Rosenblatt, 1504–1564, wife successively of Keller, Oecolampadius, Capito and Bucer)
etymology: Germanic Wibrand, war-sword, in a feminine form; German Rosenblatt, rose-leaf.
biblical_def: Wibrandis Rosenblatt was married four times and widowed four times, and three of her husbands were leading Reformers: Johannes Oecolampadius of Basel, Wolfgang Capito of Strasbourg, and Martin Bucer, with whom she went into exile in England and whom she buried at Cambridge. She brought the children of each marriage into the next household, cared for her mother, and kept open houses at Basel, Strasbourg and Cambridge in the years when every Protestant fugitive in Europe needed a bed. She died of the plague at Basel in 1564. Nobody chooses such a life. The Shunammite woman's little chamber on the wall is the biblical measure of what she did four times over, and Scripture treats the provision of a bed and a table and a stool as a service it is worth recording the details of (2Ki 4:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hospitality as the act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers, and sojourner as a temporary resident.
webster_full: HOSPITAL'ITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
SO'JOURNER, n. A temporary resident; a stranger or traveler who dwells in a place for a time.
WID'OWHOOD, n. The state of being a widow.
CHAM'BER, n. An apartment in an upper story, or in a story above the lower floor of a dwelling house.
scriptures: Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick: and it shall be, when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.

Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work.
Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
corruption_summary: Four husbands, four graves, and open houses at Basel, Strasbourg and Cambridge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of hospitality as entertaining, which is to say a pleasant option exercised when convenient. What Wibrandis Rosenblatt practised was the biblical thing: strangers in the house for months, children not her own at the table, and the work going on through bereavement and plague.

The principle to recover is that hospitality is commanded, is costly, and is recorded in Scripture with the furniture itemized. “Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick” (2Ki 4:10). The command carries an incalculable promise: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2).

pos: n. (Argula von Grumbach, c. 1492–c. 1554, Bavarian noblewoman and pamphleteer)
etymology: Germanic Argula, of uncertain derivation; von Grumbach, of the Franconian house of Grumbach.
biblical_def: Argula von Grumbach was a Bavarian noblewoman who had been given a German Bible at ten and read it. In 1523 the university of Ingolstadt forced a young student, Arsacius Seehofer, to recant his evangelical convictions under threat of death, and Argula wrote to the university, in print, challenging its theologians to show her from Scripture where the young man was wrong, and offering to debate them in German or Latin. The pamphlet went through fourteen editions in two months. Her husband was dismissed from his office for it; she was threatened, mocked in verse, and never silenced. She is the first woman to publish in defence of the Reformation in German, and she did it by doing the one thing the universities could not answer: she asked for the text (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pamphlet as a small book consisting of a few sheets, and recant as to retract a declaration or proposition.
webster_full: PAM'PHLET, n. A small book consisting of a sheet of paper, or of a few sheets stitched together but not bound.
RECANT', v.t. To retract a declaration or proposition; to recall a declaration or opinion.
CHAL'LENGE, n. An invitation or summons to fight; a calling upon one to answer for anything.
LAY, a. Pertaining to the laity or people, as distinct from the clergy.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
corruption_summary: A laywoman asked Ingolstadt for the text, and fourteen editions in two months.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary is careful here, because Argula von Grumbach is regularly enlisted as an argument for women in the teaching office, and that is not what she was doing. She did not claim an office, did not preach, and did not administer a sacrament. She was a layperson, as a man in her position would have been, demanding that teachers prove their teaching from Scripture, and the right to make that demand belongs to every member of the church without distinction of sex.

The principle to recover is that the sufficiency of Scripture puts a weapon in the hand of the humblest believer, and that using it is not usurpation. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). The Bereans did the same thing to an apostle and were commended: “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). And a child's Bible had made her able: “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15).

pos: n. (Marie Dentiere, c. 1495–1561, former abbess, writer, and controversialist of Geneva)
etymology: Hebrew Miryam, through French Marie; French Dentiere, a Tournai family name.
biblical_def: Marie Dentiere was an Augustinian abbess of Tournai who left her convent for the Reformation, married twice to Reformed ministers, and settled in Geneva. She wrote an account of the city's deliverance from the duke of Savoy and from the Roman mass, and in 1539 published an open letter to Marguerite de Navarre defending the Reformed cause and pressing the claim that women have both the right and the duty to interpret and publish Scripture. Calvin and the Geneva ministers opposed the book and it was seized. The dictionary honours her courage and her evident conversion, and does not grant her argument. The two things are separable and must be kept separate, which is what the Authorized Version itself does when it records with honour the women who laboured in the gospel while reserving the teaching office (1Ti 2:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abbess as the governess of a nunnery, and expound as to explain or interpret.
webster_full: AB'BESS, n. A female superior or governess of a nunnery or convent of nuns, having the same rank and authority over nuns that abbots have over monks.
EXPOUND', v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
SUBJEC'TION, n. The act of subduing; the state of being under the power, control and government of another.
OF'FICE, n. A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose.
scriptures: Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection.
Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law.
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.
Tit 2:3
The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;
corruption_summary: An abbess turned Reformed, honoured for her courage and answered on her claim.
corruption_paragraphs: The claim is named and rejected on scriptural grounds. Marie Dentiere argued that the restriction of public teaching to men is a human imposition that the gospel abolishes, and modern writers routinely take her side and cite her as an early witness against the complementarian reading. The texts do not permit it. Paul grounds the restriction not in custom but in the order of creation and in the law, and the churches of Corinth and Ephesus were told the same thing in two different cultures.

The principle to recover is that honour and office are not the same thing, and Scripture gives women abundant honour within a reserved order. “Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection” (1Ti 2:11). The limit is stated for the public assembly: “Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak” (1Co 14:34). And the appointed sphere is itself a teaching office: the aged women are to be “teachers of good things” (Tit 2:3), and Priscilla instructed Apollos in a house (Act 18:26).

pos: n. (Olympia Fulvia Morata, 1526–1555, Italian scholar of the Reformation)
etymology: Greek Olympia, of Olympus; Italian Morata, a Ferrarese family name.
biblical_def: Olympia Morata was the daughter of a Ferrarese humanist, lectured on Cicero at the court of Renee of France while still a girl, and was celebrated across Italy for her Greek and Latin before she was twenty. Then she was converted, and the celebration stopped. She married a German Lutheran physician, left Italy, and spent her remaining years in Germany, where she was burnt out of Schweinfurt by a siege, lost her library and her manuscripts, and died at Heidelberg at twenty-nine. What survives is her letters and some Greek verse paraphrases of the Psalms. She had traded a reputation for a confession and knew exactly what she had done. Paul's accounting of the same trade is the one she used in her own letters, and the gospel is what she counted the gain (Php 1:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines humanist as one versed in the knowledge of human nature and in classical learning, and renounce as to disown, to reject.
webster_full: HU'MANIST, n. One versed in the knowledge of human nature; a professor of grammar and rhetoric; a philologist.
RENOUNCE', v.t. To disown; to disclaim; to reject; to refuse to own or acknowledge as belonging to.
ERU'DITION, n. Learning; knowledge gained by study, or from books and instruction; particularly, learning in literature.
EX'ILE, n. The state of being expelled from one's native country; banishment.
scriptures: Php 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak;
Rom 14:8
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.
corruption_summary: A celebrated Italian scholar at twenty, burnt out of a German town, dead at twenty-nine.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the recruitment of Morata as a Renaissance prodigy whose religion was an unfortunate distraction from her learning, which is the exact inversion of her own account. She wrote that she had come to despise the things she had been praised for, not because learning is evil but because she had found something that outranked it.

The principle to recover is that reputation is a vapour and the fear of the LORD is the one commendation that survives a siege. “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Pro 31:30). Faith speaks whatever it costs: “I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak” (2Co 4:13). And the whole of her short life is covered by one clause: “whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's” (Rom 14:8).

pos: n. (Renee de France, 1510–1574, duchess of Ferrara, protector of the Reformed)
etymology: Latin renata, born again, through French Renee; a royal daughter of France.
biblical_def: Renee of France was a daughter of Louis XII, married to the duke of Ferrara, and for twenty years she kept a court in Italy where Reformed convictions could be held and Reformed fugitives could be sheltered. Calvin visited her in 1536 and corresponded with her for the rest of her life, and his letters to her are among the most searching he ever wrote, because she wavered. Under pressure from her husband, the Inquisition and her own son she conformed outwardly more than once, and Calvin told her so plainly. When widowed she returned to France, settled at Montargis, and turned the chateau into a refuge during the wars of religion, protecting hundreds. The dictionary gives her the Chronicler's kind of verdict: a mixed record, ending better than it ran, and a house that became the Shunammite's chamber on a princely scale (2Ki 4:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines protection as defence and shelter from evil, and dissemble as to hide under a false appearance.
webster_full: PROTEC'TION, n. Defense; shelter from evil; preservation from loss, injury or annoyance.
DISSEM'BLE, v.t. To hide under a false appearance; to conceal the real fact, motives, intention or sentiments.
DUCH'ESS, n. The consort or widow of a duke; also, a lady who has the sovereignty of a dukedom.
WA'VER, v.i. To fluctuate; to be unsettled in opinion; to vacillate; to be undetermined.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
corruption_summary: A French princess in Ferrara who wavered, and a chateau that sheltered hundreds.
corruption_paragraphs: The record is given whole. Renee of France protected the persecuted at real risk, and she also dissembled when the pressure came, attending the mass she had been taught to regard as idolatry in order to keep her position and her children. Calvin wrote to her about it without flattery, as he wrote to other great persons, and the dictionary follows him rather than the modern habit of treating a patron's usefulness as settling the question of her faithfulness.

The principle to recover is that protection of the persecuted is a real and commended work, and that it does not purchase exemption from the command to prove all things and hold fast what is good. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21). The shelter itself is counted: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2). And the prayer for a mixed life's work is the psalmist's: “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).

etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, in the French feminine Jeanne; d'Albret, of the house of Albret.
biblical_def: Jeanne d'Albret was queen regnant of Navarre, declared herself Reformed in 1560, and reformed her little kingdom thoroughly: the mass abolished, the Reformed worship established, pastors settled, a college founded, and the New Testament translated into Basque and into the Bearnese dialect so that her subjects could read it in the speech of their own valleys. She held Navarre against her Catholic nobles, against France, and against Spain, refused every inducement to return to Rome, and was the political anchor of the Huguenot cause until she died at Paris in 1572, two months before the massacre of St Bartholomew. She was the mother of Henry of Navarre, who later bought a throne with a mass, which is its own commentary. Deborah is the Authorized Version's word for a woman in such a place: a mother in Israel (Jdg 5:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines regnant as reigning, exercising regal authority, and vernacular as native, belonging to one's country.
webster_full: REG'NANT, a. Reigning; exercising regal authority; predominant; prevalent.
VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
QUEEN, n. The consort of a king; also, a woman who is the sovereign of a kingdom.
DI'ALECT, n. The form or idiom of a language peculiar to a province, or to a kingdom or state.
scriptures: Jdg 5:7
The inhabitants of the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel.
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
corruption_summary: She reformed Navarre and put the New Testament into Basque and Bearnese.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the reading of a queen regnant as an argument against the created order of the household and the church. It is not. Scripture records Deborah and the queen of Sheba and Esther without embarrassment and without using them to unsettle what it says elsewhere about the eldership and the home. Civil rule is a different sphere from the pulpit, and Jeanne d'Albret never confused them: she established ministers, she did not become one.

The principle to recover is that a magistrate's first service to the gospel is to get the word into the people's hands in the people's language. “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30). Paul states the rule for any utterance in the congregation: “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9). And the inheritance she was serving is not hers: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance” (Psa 2:8).

pos: n. (Marguerite d'Angouleme, 1492–1549, queen of Navarre and patron of the French evangelicals)
etymology: Greek margarites, a pearl, through French Marguerite; of Navarre, by her second marriage.
biblical_def: Marguerite de Navarre was the sister of Francis I of France and the one person at that court who could protect an evangelical. She sheltered Lefevre d'Etaples, Roussel and Briconnet, intervened for men under arrest, corresponded with the reformers, and wrote the Mirror of the Sinful Soul, a poem of such plain dependence on grace that the Sorbonne condemned it. The young Princess Elizabeth of England translated it as a schoolgirl exercise. She never broke with Rome. She kept to a reform-from-within that the next thirty years showed to be impossible, and she died with the French church unreformed and her protegees scattered or dead. The dictionary records both halves: real grace, real shelter given at real risk, and a decision not made (1Th 5:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines patron as one who countenances and supports, and temporize as to comply with the time or occasion.
webster_full: PA'TRON, n. A protector; a supporter; one who countenances, supports or protects.
TEM'PORIZE, v.i. To comply with the time or occasion; to yield to the current of opinion or to circumstances.
MIR'ROR, n. A looking glass; any glass or polished substance that forms images by the reflection of rays of light.
IN'TERCEDE, v.i. To pass between; to mediate; to plead in favor of one.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: She sheltered the French evangelicals and never broke with Rome.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the failure without erasing the service. Reform from within, which is what Marguerite and her circle attempted, assumed that Rome would correct itself if the gospel were pressed gently enough from inside. Trent settled the question. Those who had waited were left with nothing: Lefevre dead, Briconnet conformed, the French Bible men in exile or in the fire. The courage she showed in protecting individuals was genuine and the strategy was a mistake, and both are to be said.

The principle to recover is that a position must finally be taken on the testimony of Scripture, and that prolonged shelter is not a substitute for it. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21). The standard she would not quite apply is the one her own poem all but reaches: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Her charity, meanwhile, is counted: “She stretcheth out her hand to the poor” (Pro 31:20).

pos: n. (Anne Vaughan Locke, c. 1533–c. 1590, English translator and poet)
etymology: Hebrew Channah, grace, through Anne; English Locke, from her first husband's family name.
biblical_def: Anne Locke was a London merchant's daughter who sailed to Geneva in 1557 with two small children, one of whom died within days of arriving, to sit under the preaching of the exiled English church. She translated Calvin's sermons on the thirty-eighth chapter of Isaiah into English and published them in 1560, appending a sequence of sonnets on the fifty-first Psalm, which is the first sonnet sequence in English by anybody. John Knox counted her among the closest of his correspondents and wrote to her with a frankness he showed almost no one else. She later married the Puritan minister Edward Dering and then a preacher of Exeter. Her verse is a woman's confession of sin and plea for mercy set in strict metre, which is what the Psalm she chose actually is (Psa 68:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines translate as to render into another language, and sonnet as a short poem of fourteen lines.
webster_full: TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
SON'NET, n. A short poem of fourteen lines, two stanzas of four verses each, and two of three each, the rhymes being adjusted by a particular rule.
MED'ITATION, n. Close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind.
PEN'ITENT, a. Suffering pain or sorrow of heart on account of sins, crimes or offenses; contrite.
scriptures: The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak;
corruption_summary: Calvin's Isaiah sermons in English, and the first sonnet sequence in the language.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern recovery of Anne Locke purely as a literary first, with the content of what she wrote treated as the period's unavoidable packaging. The content is the thing. She chose the fifty-first Psalm, the confession of a man caught in adultery and murder, and she wrote twenty-six sonnets on it. That is not decoration; it is the doctrine of sin and grace in the hardest form English verse had yet attempted.

The principle to recover is that the word is published by many hands and that translation and sacred verse are among them. “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11). The wise woman's mouth is an instrument of instruction in its own sphere: “She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness” (Pro 31:26). And the appointed use of psalms is congregational and mutual: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).
